claims.text: The starting mixture contains multiple noble-metal precursors with different reduction tendencies.
The noble-metal precursors are combined in approximately equimolar ratios.
Synchronizing precursor reduction behaviors with a managed heating profile leads to formation of a single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticle.
Near-simultaneous metal precipitation prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
Changing temperature progression and duration can align the reduction intervals of different metals.
Aligned reduction intervals promote co-precipitation instead of sequential deposition.
A tailored stepwise process can be compared with an otherwise unchanged baseline using identical starting mixtures.
Simultaneous nucleation of all metal species into shared crystal seeds is necessary for homogeneous integration.
Staggered reduction causes early-reduced metals to form separate phases or segregated domains.
Near-concurrent reduction and nucleation allow metal atoms to mix thoroughly before crystallization.
Uncontrolled differences in precursor redox potentials or reduction rates can cause phase separation.
The synchronized condition will produce a more uniform single-phase structure than the baseline.
The synchronized condition will produce a more homogeneous elemental distribution and fewer large segregated domains than the baseline.
Without synchronization, the metals reduce at different times and form multiple phases.
Without synchronization, particles develop compositional gradients and enlarged or irregular domains.
The mechanism applies to noble-metal-containing systems whose precursor reduction windows can be made to overlap.
Extreme chemical disparities or highly reactive non-noble elements may outweigh the synchronization effect.
Unexpected synthesis behavior becomes more likely as the number of distinct elements increases.
Exact composition limits for successful synchronization are unknown.
Persistence of baseline-like multiple phases and chemical segregation after attempted synchronization would falsify the proposed requirement.
